title: CNO Financial's Third-Quarter Operating Income Jumps 41% to $179.1 Million and Guidance Is Raised, but $44.9 Million of Actuarial-Review Gains and a Lower Book Value Complicate the Picture
summary: CNO Financial Group reported third-quarter 2026 net operating income of $179.1 million, up 41%, and raised its 2026 operating EPS guidance, with $44.9 million of that coming from its annual actuarial review; reported book value per share fell to $25.34 while the statutory RBC ratio was an estimated 374%.
description:
CNO Financial Group, an Indiana-based insurer serving middle-income Americans with life, health and annuity products, reported third-quarter 2026 results on October 29 that were far stronger than a year earlier but that also contain items investors need to read carefully. According to the company's release, net operating income was $179.1 million, or $1.90 per diluted share, up 41% in dollars and 47% per share. Net income was $161.1 million, or $1.71 per diluted share, compared with $23.1 million, or $0.24, in the third quarter of 2025. For the first nine months of the year, net income was $324.7 million, or $3.41 per diluted share, against $136.4 million, or $1.36, a year earlier. The company said it was raising its 2026 operating earnings-per-share guidance, with the midpoint up 9% from the previous guidance, and that operating EPS is up 43% year to date.

What lifted the quarter

Three things shaped the result. The first is the annual actuarial review, in which insurers update the assumptions used to value long-term liabilities such as expected lapses, mortality and investment returns. CNO said the significant items from its comprehensive annual review added $44.9 million, or $0.48 per share, to both net income and net operating income. Subtracting that arithmetically from the reported $1.90 per share leaves about $1.42 per share, which is a simple calculation on the reported figures and not a company-stated number. The company's own presentation of operating return on equity makes the same point: operating ROE was 15.4%, or 14.1% excluding significant items, compared with 11.2% a year earlier.

The second factor is investment income. General account net investment income was $441.5 million, up from $382.9 million. Investment income not allocated to product lines rose 72% to $68.1 million. Income from insurance products was $172.0 million, up 15%, and insurance policy income rose to $688.2 million from $658.4 million. The third factor is the comparison: the third quarter of 2025 included a $96.7 million goodwill and asset impairment charge that depressed that period's net income, which helps explain why reported net income jumped so sharply.

Reported revenue fell, however. Total revenues were $1,086.0 million, down from $1,188.7 million, and the release shows total investment losses of $64.7 million, including realized investment losses of $48.3 million within non-operating items. Non-operating items also included a $69.7 million gain from fixed indexed annuity embedded derivatives and market risk benefits, and a $22.1 million deferred tax asset valuation allowance. These are the kind of accounting and market-driven items that explain the gap between net operating income and net income.

Sales and distribution

CNO said total new annualized premiums rose for a 17th consecutive quarter, with continued growth in asset accumulation products such as annuities. Its Consumer and Worksite agent counts grew for a 15th and 17th consecutive quarter respectively. The company describes itself as having $39.3 billion of total assets, 3.3 million policies, 3,200 associates, 5,100 exclusive agents and more than 6,500 independent partner agents. The release available for this article was truncated, so the full sales breakdown by product is not covered here.

Book value and capital

The book value figures show why insurers report several measures. Book value per share, which includes unrealized gains and losses on the bond portfolio through accumulated other comprehensive income, was $25.34 compared with $27.24 a year earlier. Book value per diluted share excluding that item was $41.29, up 8% from $38.10. The gap between the two measures reflects the accumulated other comprehensive income component. The release does not explain the drivers of the difference, and the unrealized losses are a genuine feature of the balance sheet.

On regulatory capital, CNO estimated its consolidated statutory risk-based capital ratio at 374% at September 30, 2026, and an estimated third-quarter statutory operating gain of $21.9 million. No dividends were paid by insurance subsidiaries to the holding company in the quarter. Holding company unrestricted cash and investments were $230.7 million, compared with $351.4 million at the end of 2025. The debt-to-capital ratio was 36.5%, up from 33.6% at year-end 2025, or 25.7% excluding accumulated other comprehensive income, compared with 26.2%. Those holding company liquidity and leverage figures are the ones to watch, since a holding company funds buybacks, dividends and debt service from subsidiary dividends.

Reinsurance and buybacks

A third reinsurance transaction with CNO's Bermuda affiliate closed on October 1, 2026, covering about $270 million of in-force graded benefit life statutory reserves from Colonial Penn. The release does not describe regulatory approvals or the expected capital effect.

CNO repurchased $60.0 million of its stock in the quarter, covering 1.1 million shares at an average price of $54.52. It has $240.4 million remaining on its repurchase authorisation, and 91.7 million shares were outstanding. Common dividends paid in the quarter were $16.5 million. Weighted average diluted shares for the quarter were 94.3 million.

How to read it

The results show a life insurer with improving earnings power, rising investment income and steady sales, but the headline growth is flattered by a weak comparison quarter and a favourable assumption review. Investors may weigh the lower reported book value, higher leverage and lower holding company cash against the raised guidance and strong capital ratio. The company scheduled its earnings call for October 30 at 11:00 a.m. Eastern time, where management could discuss the recurring portion of the earnings and the outlook.

This article summarises one company release, which presents management's chosen metrics and was partly truncated when reviewed. It is not investment advice, and readers should consult CNO's filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission for complete data.
image_alt: Financial documents and calculator representing life insurer earnings (illustrative)
key_points: Third-quarter net operating income was $179.1 million, or $1.90 per diluted share, up 41% in dollars and 47% per share; net income was $161.1 million against $23.1 million a year earlier.
The result includes $44.9 million, or $0.48 per share, of significant items tied to the comprehensive annual actuarial review, so the underlying improvement is smaller than the headline.
CNO raised its 2026 operating EPS guidance, with the midpoint up 9% from the prior guidance, and operating EPS is up 43% year to date.
Book value per share was $25.34 against $27.24 a year earlier, but book value per diluted share excluding accumulated other comprehensive income rose 8% to $41.29.

The estimated statutory RBC ratio was 374%, the company repurchased $60.0 million of stock in the quarter, and a third reinsurance transaction with a Bermuda affiliate closed on October 1 covering about $270 million of reserves.
why_it_matters: CNO sells life, health and annuity products largely to middle-income Americans through exclusive and independent agents, so its results show how a mid-sized life insurer is balancing growth in annuity sales, investment income and capital management. The way the quarter's profit leans on an actuarial review is a reminder to separate recurring earnings from one-time assumption updates.

title: Erie Indemnity's Third-Quarter Net Income Holds at $182.0 Million as Management Fees Rise 2.6% and Higher Agent Incentives Take Commissions Up $24 Million
summary: Erie Indemnity reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $182.0 million, or $3.48 per diluted share, almost level with a year earlier, as higher management fees were offset by a $24.0 million rise in commissions and a Class A dividend of $1.4625 per share.
description:
Erie Indemnity Company reported third-quarter 2026 results on October 29 that show a steady fee business. Net income was $182.0 million, or $3.48 per diluted share, compared with $182.9 million, or $3.50 per diluted share, in the third quarter of 2025. For the first nine months, net income was $512.8 million, or $9.80 per diluted share, up from $496.0 million, or $9.48. The company is often described alongside property and casualty insurers, but its income statement works differently, which is why the numbers need a short explanation before the figures themselves.

What Erie Indemnity does

Erie Indemnity acts as the management company for the Erie Insurance Exchange, a reciprocal insurer owned by its policyholders. The Exchange takes the underwriting risk and holds the claims reserves; Erie Indemnity provides services such as sales, underwriting and policy issuance, and it earns fees for them. Those fees are the main source of its revenue. The release lists two categories: management fees for policy issuance and renewal, and management fees for administrative services. Because the fees are linked to premiums written by the Exchange, Erie Indemnity's results depend on premium growth and expense control, not on catastrophe losses, which fall mainly on the Exchange. The release does not include results for the Exchange or a combined ratio, so those cannot be assessed from it.

Fees and operating income

Management fees for policy issuance and renewal rose $21.7 million, or 2.6%, in the third quarter, and $92.1 million, or 3.8%, over nine months. Management fees for administrative services rose $0.9 million, or 4.7%, in the quarter and $4.0 million, or 7.4%, over nine months. Despite the fee growth, third-quarter operating income fell $1.5 million, or 0.7%. Nine-month operating income rose $18.8 million, or 3.4%.

The reason operating income was flat is on the cost side. Commissions rose $24.0 million in the quarter. The company said this was primarily driven by an increase in agent incentive compensation and by the growth in direct and affiliated assumed written premium. Agent incentive compensation is paid to independent agents who meet targets for growth and profitability, so a rise suggests the agency force achieved more of its goals or that the incentive structure has been enhanced. The release does not give the size of premium growth that triggered the payments, so the connection between premium growth and agent pay cannot be quantified here.

Investment income

Total investment income was $19.9 million in the third quarter compared with $21.6 million a year earlier. Within that, net investment income rose to $25.4 million from $21.0 million, but net realized and unrealized losses of $5.4 million reduced the total. Investment results are a small part of Erie Indemnity's earnings compared with fees, though they can swing the bottom line in a quarter when markets move.

Dividends and balance sheet

Dividends are a central part of the Erie Indemnity investment case. Class A dividends declared were $1.4625 per share in the third quarter, up from $1.365, and $4.3875 per share for the nine months, up from $4.095. By simple arithmetic on the quarterly figures, that is an increase of about 7% per share. The release does not say how many shares are outstanding in total or give the payout ratio, so the dividend's cost to the company cannot be calculated from it.

At September 30, 2026, total assets were $3.66 billion and shareholders' equity was $2.55 billion. The release does not contain guidance, share repurchase information or details of the Exchange's premiums or loss ratios.

Reading the quarter

The quarter shows a mature fee model. Fee growth of between 2.6% and 4.7% in the quarter is steady rather than rapid, and it is largely absorbed by commissions and other costs. The nine-month view is somewhat stronger, with operating income up 3.4%. The increase in dividends signals confidence in cash generation, but with no guidance in the release it is hard to tell what the company expects for the fourth quarter.

For readers who follow the property and casualty sector, Erie Indemnity is a reminder that not every insurance-related stock has direct exposure to claims. In years of heavy storms, the Exchange can report weaker underwriting results while the management company's fees continue, though the Exchange's financial strength is still important to the long-term franchise because the fee depends on the Exchange continuing to write business. In years of soft pricing, slower premium growth can weigh on fees even if claims are benign.

What to watch next

Investors will look for the Exchange's own results, which are filed separately, and for any comment on pricing, policy counts and agent incentives. The release excerpt does not discuss the commission rate or the management fee rate.

This article summarises a company press release and is general information, not investment advice. Readers who rely on these figures should consult Erie Indemnity's filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

key_points: Third-quarter net income was $182.0 million, or $3.48 per diluted share, against $182.9 million, or $3.50, a year earlier; nine-month net income was $512.8 million, or $9.80 per share.
Management fees for policy issuance and renewal rose $21.7 million, or 2.6%, in the quarter and $92.1 million, or 3.8%, over nine months.
Commissions rose $24.0 million in the quarter, which the company attributes mainly to higher agent incentive compensation and growth in direct and affiliated assumed written premium.
Class A dividends declared were $1.4625 per share for the quarter, up from $1.365, and $4.3875 for nine months, up from $4.095.
Total assets were $3.66 billion and shareholders' equity was $2.55 billion at September 30, 2026; the release gives no guidance, buyback or Erie Insurance Exchange results.
why_it_matters: Erie Indemnity is not the insurer that bears the risk: it earns fees for managing the Erie Insurance Exchange, so its income tracks premium growth and agent costs more than catastrophe losses or reserves. That makes its results a useful read on how much the system around the Exchange is growing and on the cost of keeping agents motivated.

title: Ontario Regulator Finds Two-Thirds of Sampled Life Agents Skipped Needs and Suitability Assessments, and Warns Insurers That 'Delegation Does Not Mean Abdication'
summary: Phase 1 of Ontario regulator FSRA's review of insurer and MGA relationships found that 66% of 50 sampled life agents did not complete needs and suitability assessments, 74% gave no policy illustrations and 53% gave incomplete disclosures, and that insurers reviewed 0% to 4% of their active agents.
description:
Ontario's financial services regulator has produced one of the more pointed market-conduct findings on life insurance distribution in recent years. In the first phase of a review of how insurers manage their relationships with managing general agencies, known as MGAs, the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario, FSRA, found that most of the agents it examined had not completed basic steps designed to protect buyers. The findings were reported by Insurance Business Canada on October 27, 2026. They rest on FSRA's supervisory review and on data provided by the insurers themselves, which the regulator did not independently verify, and FSRA says the work is ongoing.

Who was reviewed

FSRA looked at eight life and health insurers that together hold about 65% of the Ontario market by direct written premiums, so the sample covers most of the market, although it is a small number of companies. It examined 50 life agents working through 10 MGAs and analysed 47 client files. An MGA is an intermediary to which an insurer delegates functions such as recruiting, contracting and supporting agents. Many insurers rely on MGAs to distribute products without building their own sales forces, which is why the relationship between insurer and MGA is a supervisory priority.

What FSRA found about agents

The conduct findings are stark. Some 66% of the agents examined had not completed needs and suitability assessments, the process by which an agent gathers information about a client's circumstances and checks that the recommended product fits. Some 74% had not provided policy illustrations, which show how a product is expected to perform and what it will cost under stated assumptions. And 53% had not provided complete adviser disclosures, the information that tells a client who the agent is, how the agent is paid and what conflicts of interest might exist. These are percentages of a sample of 50, so each agent represents two percentage points, and the sample was not described as random; the numbers should not be read as a statistic for all Ontario agents.

What FSRA found about insurers

The second set of findings concerns oversight. All eight insurers delegated at least some agent recruiting, screening, training or monitoring to MGAs. Only four had documented supervision policies covering all of the MGAs they had contracted. Insurers' own proactive reviews of agents covered between 0% and 4% of their active agents. In other words, the firms that carry the regulatory responsibility were looking at a very small share of the people selling their products.

FSRA also found that every participating insurer worked with at least one MGA using a multi-level marketing model, which rewards agents for recruiting other agents, and that in some cases a large share of an insurer's business came through such an MGA. The regulator noted that its earlier reviews had raised similar concerns about rapid growth and incentives to expand recruiting networks. The concern about multi-level structures is that rewards for recruiting can overshadow the quality of the advice given to customers.

The core message

The article quotes the central message for insurers: delegation does not mean abdication. FSRA is examining the gap between what insurer and MGA agreements require and how they operate in practice. If an agreement requires suitability assessments but nobody checks that they happen, the contract does not protect customers.

The licensing question

The review lands amid uncertainty about how MGAs will be regulated. According to the report, Ontario's planned MGA licensing regime, which had been targeted for June 1, 2026, was paused in February after the industry warned that its definition of an MGA was too broad. A Finance Ministry consultation paper in July proposed amendments to the Insurance Act to narrow the scope. The result is that a licensing framework is still not in force while the regulator is documenting the issues it was meant to address.

Next steps

FSRA said it is expanding its questionnaire to six more insurers, which will broaden the sample. It plans a separate review of recruitment practices, which is where multi-level marketing structures are most relevant, and it will assess the service provided for orphaned life policies. Orphaned policies are typically those whose selling agent is no longer servicing them, and the risks FSRA names include lapses, outdated beneficiaries and weaker claims readiness. A policyholder whose agent has moved on may have nobody to call when circumstances change.

What it means for consumers

Consumers buying life insurance in Ontario can protect themselves by asking for a written needs assessment, a policy illustration and an adviser disclosure document, and by keeping copies. They can ask how the agent is paid and whether the agent works through an MGA. If they feel they were sold an unsuitable product, they can complain to the insurer and, if unsatisfied, escalate to the relevant ombudsman service. The article does not give specific complaint routes, so consumers should check with FSRA for current details.

What it means for insurers and MGAs

Insurers can expect more scrutiny of their supervision frameworks, their sampling of agent files and their treatment of recruiting incentives. Practical steps include documenting supervision policies for every MGA, increasing the share of agents reviewed, testing whether suitability and illustration requirements are followed, and examining whether compensation structures encourage recruitment at the expense of advice quality. MGAs should expect information requests and should be ready to evidence compliance.

Limits of the findings

FSRA's own caveats are important. The data are self-reported by insurers, the reviewed group is small, and this is Phase 1 of a continuing programme. No enforcement outcomes are described in the report. This article summarises a trade-press report of a regulatory publication and is general information, not legal or financial advice.
source_name: Insurance Business Canada (October 27, 2026), reporting on FSRA's Phase 1 observations
image_alt: Documents and a pen representing insurance suitability paperwork (illustrative)
key_points: FSRA reviewed insurer and managing general agency (MGA) relationships at eight life and health insurers holding about 65% of Ontario's market by direct written premiums.

Of 50 life agents examined across 10 MGAs, with 47 client files analysed, 66% did not complete needs and suitability assessments, 74% did not provide policy illustrations and 53% did not give complete adviser disclosures.

All eight insurers delegated some agent recruiting, screening, training or monitoring to MGAs, but only four had documented supervision policies covering all their contracted MGAs, and insurers' own reviews covered 0% to 4% of active agents.
Every participating insurer worked with at least one MGA using a multi-level marketing model that rewards recruiting.

FSRA will extend its questionnaire to six more insurers, review recruitment practices separately and assess service for orphaned life policies; the findings rely on self-reported insurer data that FSRA did not independently verify.
why_it_matters: Life insurance is sold on trust, and suitability assessments and illustrations are the main protections for buyers. If a majority of sampled agents skipped them, and insurers were not checking, consumers could end up with unsuitable policies. For insurers, the message is that outsourcing distribution to MGAs does not outsource responsibility.

title: Ontario Court Approves a C$213.5 Million Sun Life Universal Life Settlement, Which Class Counsel Calls the Largest of Its Kind in Canada, With Cost-of-Insurance Freezes for Flexiplus Holders
summary: The Ontario Superior Court has approved a C$213.5 million national class action settlement in Fehr v. Sun Life over three legacy universal life products sold by MetLife agents between 1987 and 1998, with direct payments, a permanent freeze on Flexiplus charges and a cap on future Universal Plus costs of insurance.
description:
An Ontario court has approved a settlement that class counsel describes as the largest reported in a Canadian life insurance policy dispute. According to Insurance Business Canada, which reported the approval on October 28, 2026, the Ontario Superior Court of Justice approved a C$213.5 million national class action settlement in the case of Fehr et al. v. Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada. The court found the deal fair, reasonable and in the best interests of the class. The case began in 2010 and the Ontario Court of Appeal certified the class in 2018, so the approval ends a dispute that has run for sixteen years. Sun Life disputes that it did anything wrong.

What the case is about

The lawsuit concerns the alleged improper administration of three universal life policies: Universal Plus, Flexiplus and OptiMet. Universal life is a type of permanent life insurance in which the policyholder pays premiums into an account, the insurer deducts charges, including a cost of insurance and administration fees, and interest is credited. The insurer can change some of those charges within limits set in the contract, which makes the contract wording central to disputes. According to the report, MetLife agents sold these policies in Canada between 1987 and 1998. Sun Life says it inherited them through earlier Canadian acquisitions and that it sold none of the products at issue.

For Universal Plus policies, the claims centre on the term Maximum Premium in earlier policy versions. According to the report, certain current and former holders of policies issued before 1992 may receive compensation if their cost of insurance charges exceeded the stated base coverage Maximum Premium. For Flexiplus, the claims relate to increases in cost of insurance and administration fees.

Who is in the class

The class consists of current and former Flexiplus and Universal Plus policyholders, about 70,000 people in total. The report notes that Daily Hive, citing the class action website, said OptiMet class members are no longer included, so people with OptiMet policies should check the settlement website or class counsel before assuming they are covered. The article does not describe a claims procedure, any deadlines or how eligibility will be confirmed, so those details must come from the official settlement notice.

What policyholders receive

Eligible current and former Flexiplus policyholders will receive direct payments covering part of past increases in cost of insurance and administration fees. For current Flexiplus holders, cost of insurance rates and administration fees will be permanently frozen. For current Universal Plus holders with policies issued before 1992, future cost of insurance charges will be capped at a set multiple of the Maximum Premium amount. The report does not give individual payment amounts or the multiple that applies, so it is not possible to say what any one policyholder might receive. Total settlement value includes both cash and the forward-looking limits on charges, and the article does not split the C$213.5 million between them.

Counsel and quotes

Class counsel is Kim Spencer McPhee Barristers P.C., whose managing principal Megan B. McPhee described it as the largest reported settlement in a Canadian life insurance policy dispute. She said the settlement will put money back in class members' pockets. Representative plaintiff Eldon Fehr said he was pleased to see the litigation finally come to a close. These statements come from the plaintiffs' side; the report does not include a comment from Sun Life beyond its position that it did nothing wrong and its intention to pursue recourse.

The financial side for Sun Life

On April 30, 2026, Sun Life announced a settlement in principle and said it expected a charge of about C$145 million to first-quarter net income. The difference between the C$145 million charge and the C$213.5 million headline figure is not explained in the article, and it should not be assumed that the two numbers are comparable, since the charge may be net of other items. Sun Life says it will seek full recourse from MetLife under an indemnity if the court approves the deal. How MetLife responds, and whether the indemnity will cover the full amount, is not stated in the report and may be a separate dispute.

Why legacy policies create liability

The case illustrates a recurring issue in the life insurance industry. Policies sold decades ago were written with charges the insurer could adjust, and disputes arise when policyholders question whether the adjustments were permitted. Insurers that acquire books of business also acquire the contractual obligations and the legal risk, even if they did not originally sell the product. For acquirers, indemnities from sellers are therefore a crucial part of deal protection, which is why the reference to MetLife matters.

What to do if you hold one of these policies

Policyholders who think they may be in the class should look for the official notice from the court or class counsel, check the policy name and issue date, and keep their policy documents and statements. They should be cautious of unsolicited offers to file claims for a fee, since a court-approved settlement process normally has its own free claims route, although this article does not specify the one that applies here.

This article summarises one trade-press report on a court approval and is general information, not legal advice. The settlement notice and court documents are the authoritative sources.
image_alt: Courthouse columns representing a court-approved class action settlement (illustrative)
key_points: The Ontario Superior Court of Justice approved a C$213.5 million settlement in Fehr et al. v. Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada, a case that began in 2010.

It concerns the alleged improper administration of the Universal Plus, Flexiplus and OptiMet universal life policies sold by MetLife agents in Canada from 1987 to 1998; Sun Life says it inherited them through acquisitions and disputes any wrongdoing.
The class covers current and former Flexiplus and Universal Plus policyholders, about 70,000 people; Daily Hive, citing the class action website, reported that OptiMet members are no longer included.

Eligible Flexiplus holders receive direct payments toward past cost-of-insurance and administration fee increases, those charges are permanently frozen for current Flexiplus holders, and future Universal Plus charges for current pre-1992 holders are capped.

Sun Life announced a settlement in principle on April 30 with an expected charge of about C$145 million to first-quarter net income and says it will seek full recourse from MetLife under an indemnity.
why_it_matters: Universal life policies let insurers adjust charges over decades, and disputes over how those charges were set can take years to resolve. The settlement shows the scale of liability that can attach to old policy wording, and it matters to policyholders deciding whether they are in the class and to insurers that have acquired legacy books.

title: Alberta's Care-First Auto Model Starts January 1: 90% of Net Income Replaced, Up to $306,580 for Catastrophic Injuries, and a Projected Average Saving of About $297
summary: Alberta's Care-First auto model replaces lawsuits with no-fault benefits from January 1, 2027, offering income replacement of 90% of net income, treatment until maximum medical recovery and lump sums that Intact estimates at up to $306,580, with the rate board projecting average savings of about $297 a vehicle.
description:
Alberta is about to change the way people injured in car crashes are compensated, and the change reaches every driver in the province. Under the Care-First model, which takes effect on January 1, 2027, the court-based system for injury claims is replaced by a no-fault benefits system that applies automatically to Alberta collisions from that date. Insurance Business Canada, in a report published on October 28, 2026, set out the numbers brokers will need to explain, and renewal notices priced under the new model have been going out since November 1. This article summarises that report. Individual outcomes will depend on the policy and the circumstances, and the official government and insurer materials are the authoritative source.

Income replacement

Under the current system, an injured driver receives the lower of $600 a week or 80% of average gross earnings, for up to two years, and longer claims have to go through the courts. Under Care-First, income replacement is 90% of net income, subject to a maximum gross yearly income that is adjusted every year, and it is payable until age 65. The report cites Intact's estimate that the 2027 cap will be $128,000. After age 65 a retirement income benefit applies, and higher earners can buy additional income protection. For someone who earns more than the cap, the benefit is calculated on the capped amount, which is why the report lists the question of whether the cap leaves high earners underinsured as one that brokers should expect, and suggests that optional additional cover or disability insurance may be relevant.

Medical and rehabilitation care

The current system limits medical and rehabilitation benefits with a cap. Care-First replaces the cap with coverage for necessary treatment until maximum medical recovery. Benefits also cover personal care assistance and travel and accommodation connected with treatment. Caregiver benefits, childcare expense reimbursement and death and funeral benefits are also part of the package. This matters for people with serious injuries whose treatment costs can exceed a fixed cap, but the report does not describe how disputes about what is necessary will be decided.

Permanent impairment payments

For lasting, life-altering injuries, Care-First provides a one-time payment. The government describes it as serving a purpose similar to pain and suffering damages in the court system. Intact's estimates for 2027 maximums are $306,580 for catastrophic injuries and $194,159 for non-catastrophic injuries. These are maximums, not typical payments, and the report does not state the payments for lesser impairments or how the amounts are assessed.

A rough comparison with the current system

The report's figures allow a simple comparison for the income benefit. Under the current system, the maximum weekly benefit is $600, and it lasts up to two years. Multiplying $600 by 52 weeks and two years gives a ceiling of $62,400 in total, which is arithmetic on the reported terms and not a figure from the report. Care-First's benefit, by contrast, is a percentage of net income, up to a cap on gross yearly income, and it can continue until age 65. For a younger worker with a long-term injury, the difference in duration could be considerable, while for a person with a short recovery the difference may be small. The report does not model these cases, so individual outcomes will depend on income, age and the nature of the injury.

The same logic applies to treatment. A cap on medical and rehabilitation benefits can run out before treatment ends, whereas cover until maximum medical recovery depends on what is judged necessary. Neither system is risk-free for the injured person: one limits the amount, the other relies on the decisions made about what treatment is needed.

Fault and driving records

Moving away from lawsuits does not mean fault disappears. At-fault drivers can still face higher premiums, demerit points and charges. The change is in how injured people are compensated, not in the consequences of causing a crash. A client may ask what happens if they are injured and the other driver is at fault; the report lists this as a question brokers should be ready for, since under a no-fault model the injured person generally claims benefits from their own policy, but readers should check the official explanation for the exact rules.

What will drivers pay?

The Automobile Insurance Rate Board projects average savings of about $297 per private passenger vehicle, with larger reductions for young drivers. The report stresses that individual premiums depend on driving record, vehicle and coverage choices, so a client's renewal can differ from the advertised average. Readers should check the rate board's latest materials for the current projection.

The Alberta Civil Trial Lawyers Association has questioned the savings projections and argued that limiting lawsuits reduces access to full compensation. That disagreement is central to the policy debate: supporters point to lower premiums and faster access to treatment, while critics say people lose the right to seek full damages. The report presents the criticism without assessing it, and this article does not take a side.

Three questions brokers should expect

The report highlights three client questions. First, why does a client's renewal differ from the advertised average? The answer lies in the individual rating factors. Second, what happens if the client is injured and the other driver was at fault? Third, does the income cap leave high earners underinsured? Brokers should prepare clear answers, documents and examples, and clients should ask them before January.

Practical steps for drivers

Drivers can compare their renewal with last year's, ask their broker how the change affects each coverage, check whether they have disability or critical illness cover that would complement the benefits, and review whether optional additional income protection is worth buying. Families should ask about benefits for dependants and caregivers. Self-employed drivers and those with irregular income should ask how net income will be determined.

This article is a summary of one trade-press report and is general information, not insurance or legal advice.
image_alt: Cars on a road representing auto insurance in Alberta (illustrative)
key_points: Care-First takes effect January 1, 2027, replacing the court-based injury model, and renewal notices priced under it have been sent since November 1.

Income replacement is 90% of net income up to a maximum gross yearly income adjusted annually, payable until age 65; Intact estimates the 2027 cap at $128,000, compared with the current lower of $600 a week or 80% of average gross earnings for up to two years.

Medical and rehabilitation cover continues until maximum medical recovery, replacing a cap, and a one-time permanent impairment payment is estimated by Intact at up to $306,580 for catastrophic injuries and $194,159 for non-catastrophic injuries.

The Automobile Insurance Rate Board projects average savings of about $297 per private passenger vehicle, with larger reductions for young drivers, while the Alberta Civil Trial Lawyers Association questions the projections.

At-fault drivers can still face higher premiums, demerit points and charges, and brokers should expect questions on why renewals differ from the advertised average and whether the income cap leaves high earners underinsured.
why_it_matters: Every Alberta driver will be insured under a different injury system from January 1, which changes what an injured person can claim and what drivers pay. The advertised average saving may not match an individual renewal, and high earners and anyone who might have sued after a crash need to understand what the new benefits do and do not cover.

title: AXA's Nine-Month Premiums Rise 5% to €93 Billion as AXA XL Shrinks 1% in a Softening Market, Hail Losses Breach the Cat Budget and the Solvency II Ratio Slips to 213%
summary: AXA reported nine-month 2026 premiums and other revenues up 5% to €93 billion, with AXA XL's insurance business down 1% on lower prices, natural catastrophe losses above budget after hailstorms in France, Switzerland and Italy, a Solvency II ratio of 213%, and full-year underlying earnings guidance of about €8.6 billion.
description:
AXA's nine-month results, reported by Insurance Business on October 29, 2026, describe a large European insurer growing in personal and retail lines while deliberately holding back in the part of its business most exposed to falling commercial prices. Group premiums and other revenues rose 5% to €93 billion. Property and casualty gross written premiums and other revenues reached €48.1 billion, up 3% on a comparable basis, which means after adjusting for currency and changes in the scope of the group. The figures come from a trade-press summary of AXA's release, so some of the company's other disclosures are not covered here.

Where the growth came from

Personal lines were the strongest part of the P&C portfolio, growing 7% to €17.2 billion. Retail P&C and commercial business outside AXA XL grew 6% overall. AXA XL, the group's global large-commercial and reinsurance unit, moved the other way: its insurance business shrank 1%. The report says prices fell 1% in AXA XL's insurance business, that property volumes rose and that casualty volumes fell. AXA described this as disciplined cycle management in a softening market. The idea is that when prices fall, a disciplined insurer writes less business rather than accepting terms it considers inadequate, giving up premium to protect margins.

The retreat is sharper in reinsurance. AXA XL Reinsurance premiums fell 9% to €2.2 billion. This article is based only on the AXA report and does not assess the wider reinsurance market.

Hail and the catastrophe budget

Natural catastrophe losses exceeded the prorated annual budget of 4.5 points of combined ratio. A point of combined ratio is one percentage point of premiums earned, so a 4.5-point budget means the group plans for natural catastrophe claims to take about 4.5% of premiums over the year. The report attributes the overshoot to secondary perils, which are smaller or more frequent events such as hail, floods and storms that are not the headline disasters, mainly in France, Switzerland and Italy.

The modelling firm PERILS estimated insured losses from the late-August Raphaela hailstorms at €3.3 billion, after €2.2 billion from July storms in the same countries. Together that is €5.5 billion of insured losses from two hail episodes, a simple sum of the two reported estimates, and it is for the industry as a whole, not for AXA alone. The report does not state AXA's own share of those losses or the exact size of the overshoot against the budget, so the hit to AXA's earnings cannot be quantified from it.

The report does not discuss the causes of the hail losses, and this article draws no attribution beyond what the source says.

Capital and guidance

AXA's Solvency II ratio, the European regulatory measure of capital strength, fell to 213% at the end of September from 218% at the end of June. A ratio above 100% means the group holds more eligible capital than the regulatory requirement, so 213% is well above the minimum, and a five-point move over a quarter is modest. The report does not say what drove the decline, so the reasons cannot be determined from it.

AXA's guidance is for full-year underlying earnings of about €8.6 billion, with underlying earnings per share growth at the top end of its 6% to 8% target range. This indicates the company expects to meet its objectives despite the catastrophe overshoot. The report does not provide the breakdown of how the group expects to get there.

What it means for customers and brokers

For policyholders, the picture depends on the line. Personal and retail customers are seeing premium growth, which in the report appears as higher volumes and higher revenue, not necessarily as price rises, since the figures combine both effects. For large commercial buyers, the report shows AXA XL prices down 1%, with property volumes up and casualty volumes down.

For the market, the AXA results highlight the tension between two forces. A soft market encourages price competition and growth in volumes, but weather losses have not softened. Insurers that manage the cycle by cutting volume where margins are thin are accepting lower growth in return for earnings stability.

How to read the numbers together

The figures can be read as three separate stories. The first is growth: group revenue of €93 billion, up 5%, and P&C revenue of €48.1 billion, up 3% on a comparable basis, show a business still expanding. The second is a deliberate choice about price: AXA XL, where prices fell 1%, is the part of the group that grew least, with the insurance business down 1% and reinsurance down 9%. The third is weather: the hail losses show that even in a softening market, claims for secondary perils can accumulate and push a company beyond its budget.

The three stories interact. Falling commercial prices reduce the margin available to absorb weather losses, which is one reason a disciplined insurer reduces volume in the segments where prices are weakest. The report presents AXA's approach as a decision to hold back; it does not say whether the approach has improved margins, and the nine-month figures alone cannot show that.

It is also worth remembering the different measures used. Premiums and other revenues are a measure of the size of the business, underlying earnings are a measure of profit before certain items, and the Solvency II ratio is a measure of capital. A company can report growth in the first, guidance for the second and a small decline in the third in the same release, as AXA does, without any contradiction.

Limits of the source

This article relies on one trade-press report of the results. It does not include the full AXA release, segment profit figures, the reserve position or the dividend, and it should not be taken as a complete view of the company. It is general information and not investment advice. Readers who need detail should refer to AXA's published results and regulatory filings.
